section_summary: This section contains explanatory material and two translations of Japan’s 1939 ordinance regulating the entry, transit, residence, registration, travel, departure, and deportation of aliens, followed by correspondence assessing its compatibility with American and British treaty rights. Later documents address amendments to the ordinance, reciprocal rules for passengers landing temporarily from ships, and consular guarantees for travelers lacking Japanese visas. The final pages concern earlier visa difficulties involving Ralph and Elien Caples, an inquiry by Maurine Carley, and the Marcus Show’s reliance on transit visas under the 1926 reciprocal visa-waiver agreement.

subfiles.title: Explanation of revisions governing the entry, sojourn, and departure of foreigners
subfiles.from: Japanese Foreign Office, translated or summarized for the American Embassy
subfiles.about: Explains the principal changes introduced by Japan’s new ordinance controlling foreigners.
subfiles.summary: The continuation describes permits and fees for stays of thirty days or more, residence reports for stays of sixty days or more, and travel certificates for foreign residents visiting Manchukuo or China. It also covers advance notice of departure, expanded prefectural deportation powers, and new criminal and administrative penalties. Diplomatic and consular personnel are not expressly exempted, but their customary treatment is said to remain unchanged.

subfiles.title: Tentative Translation of Home Department Ordinance No. 6 concerning the Entry, Sojourn and Departure of Foreigners
subfiles.from: Japanese Ministry of Home Affairs
subfiles.about: Sets out the complete regulations governing foreign entry, transit, residence, registration, travel, departure, deportation, fees, and penalties.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance defines entry and transit, specifies inadmissible classes, and requires passports or equivalent documentation, visas, and police examination. It establishes special-entry and transit permits, sojourn permissions, lodging and residence reporting, residence and travel certificates, and departure notices. It authorizes deportation and prescribes fines, detention, or imprisonment for violations. The ordinance took effect on May 1, 1939, and repealed the January 1918 ordinance.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note on Tokyo’s alien-ordinance despatch
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes the new Japanese ordinance and flags the accompanying treaty correspondence for legal review.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern note: the ordinance is chiefly police regulation of foreigners; the Embassy's view that it is not inconsistent with American treaty rights is reasonable, with enforcement problems to be reported.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3868: Translation of Ordinance Relating to Alien’s Entry, Sojourn, and Departure
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits the Embassy’s translation of the new Japanese alien-control ordinance and analyzes its purpose and treaty implications.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that Ordinance No. 6 was promulgated March 1 and took effect May 1, 1939, replacing the 1918 ordinance in Japan proper. He attributes the revision to national mobilization and the desire to formalize procedures developed over the preceding decades, then summarizes its principal changes. The despatch also discusses British concern that the rules might violate treaty residence rights and concludes that the ordinance is not inherently inconsistent with American treaty rights, provided it is not applied discriminatorily.

subfiles.title: Embassy translation of Ministry of Home Affairs Ordinance No. 6
subfiles.from: Koichi Kido, Minister for Home Affairs, and Hachiro Arita, Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: General public; enclosed with Despatch No. 3868
subfiles.about: Provides the American Embassy’s full translation of Japan’s 1939 ordinance on alien entry, sojourn, and departure.
subfiles.summary: The translation establishes documentary and police-examination requirements, special entry and transit permissions, limits on transit and sojourn, and detailed lodging and residence reports. It also governs residence and travel certificates, police questioning, fees, departure notices, deportation, and punishment. The supplementary regulations make the ordinance effective May 1, 1939, and repeal the January 1918 rule.

subfiles.title: New Aliens Registration Ordinance and Treaties
subfiles.from: L. H. Gourley, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports British objections that the new registration ordinance may violate treaty rights of residence.
subfiles.summary: Gourley reports the British consulate at Kobe received complaints the ordinance violates the 1911 Anglo-Japanese treaty; one American resident thinks protests would be futile.

subfiles.title: Reply to L. H. Gourley on treaty compatibility of the alien ordinance
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador
subfiles.to: L. H. Gourley, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Explains why the alien-registration ordinance does not on its face violate American treaty rights and requests monitoring for discriminatory enforcement.
subfiles.summary: Grew tells Gourley the treaty's liberty to reside is tied to trade, so the procedure is neither inconsistent nor discriminatory; report any infringement of American rights.

subfiles.title: Legal Adviser memorandum on Japanese law governing the entry, sojourn, and departure of aliens
subfiles.from: Department of State, Office of the Legal Adviser
subfiles.about: Concurs that the Japanese law does not itself violate United States treaty rights and recommends no protest.
subfiles.summary: The Legal Adviser agrees there is no present basis for a US protest; the consul is monitoring administration for discrimination against Americans.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3969: Transmission of translation of ordinance revising alien-entry rules
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits Ordinance No. 22, which expands exemptions from alien entry, transit, and sojourn fees.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 3969: the amendment exempts aliens who paid fees in Japan's territories and travel through Japan, and lets the Home Minister grant other exemptions.

subfiles.title: Translation of Ministry of Home Affairs Ordinance No. 22
subfiles.from: Koichi Kido, Minister for Home Affairs, and Hachiro Arita, Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: General public; enclosed with Despatch No. 3969
subfiles.about: Amends Article 15 of Ordinance No. 6 by expanding exemptions from entry, transit, and sojourn fees.
subfiles.summary: Ministry of Home Affairs Ordinance No. 22 keeps exemptions for children under fifteen and force majeure and adds travelers who paid fees in Japanese territories.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for file 894.111
subfiles.from: Department of State records staff
subfiles.about: Records an administrative charge or temporary removal of material from file 894.111.
subfiles.summary: Charge slip for file 894.111 (enclosure), dated October 6, 1941; other details illegible.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: American missionaries’ difficulties obtaining residence permits
subfiles.from: Nagoya (Stephan)
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a Nagoya despatch reporting missionaries’ difficulties with Japanese police over residence permits.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Nagoya Despatch No. 280 (July 10, 1939) on American missionaries' difficulties with police over residence permits.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Legal status of American residents not covered by treaty provisions
subfiles.from: Japan (Cameron)
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch concerning the legal status in Japan of American residents outside treaty protection.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 518 (July 29, 1939) on American residents whose legal status was not covered by treaty provisions.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4183: Revision of Japanese-American reciprocal arrangement for temporary landings
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the revision of reciprocal rules for through-passengers landing temporarily while their vessels are in port.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 4183: the 1922 arrangement let through-passengers land without visas; after US limited entry certificates, Japan applied amended Ordinance No. 6 to Americans from December 1, 1939.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Mr. Yamazaki
subfiles.from: American Third Secretary Schuler
subfiles.about: Records a Foreign Office inquiry into whether new United States documentation rules had displaced the 1922 reciprocal landing agreement.
subfiles.summary: Yamazaki says the 1922 notes let ship passengers land temporarily without visas; the American Consulate General's letter seemed to cancel it, and Japan would withdraw it from Americans if the US considers it superseded.

subfiles.title: Letter explaining United States limited entry certificates
subfiles.from: C. R. Cameron, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Explains the new American requirement that temporary through-passengers possess limited entry certificates.
subfiles.summary: Cameron explains US limited entry certificates: through-passengers need a free certificate from an American consulate, showing departure within ten days via the same port and vessel.

subfiles.title: Note No. 1385 on Executive Order 8029 and temporary landings
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.to: Kichisaburo Nomura, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Notifies Japan that Executive Order 8029 requires temporary nonimmigrant visitors to present limited entry certificates.
subfiles.summary: Note No. 1385: Executive Order 8029 now requires a limited entry certificate, instead of a visaed passport, for nonimmigrants landing temporarily up to ten days at the same port.

subfiles.title: Note No. 116, American III, on Japanese documentation for temporary landings
subfiles.from: Kichisaburo Nomura, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Responds to the American documentation change by requiring Americans landing temporarily in Japan to obtain Japanese visas or permits.
subfiles.summary: Nomura cites Japan's amended Ordinance No. 6: unvisaed travelers staying up to fourteen days need a ten-yen transit certificate, fifteen days or more a twenty-yen permit; Americans should obtain visas from December 1, 1939.

subfiles.title: Department instruction on guarantees for Americans arriving in Japan without visas
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Clarifies that a Department request to assist an unvisaed traveler does not authorize a consular officer to assume financial responsibility.
subfiles.summary: Instruction on the Ralph Caples case: failing to obtain a Japanese visa is the traveler's responsibility, and a cable request does not authorize consular financial guarantees.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 305: Japanese passport requirements for Mr. and Mrs. Ralph Caples
subfiles.doc_type: consular despatch with internal processing sheet
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports the Caples landing and asks whether a Department cable authorized the Consulate to sign Japan’s required guarantee.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 305: the shipping line had arranged landing for Ralph and Elien Caples without visas. Boyce asks if a guarantee may be signed; Garrels recommends only under explicit instructions.

subfiles.title: Translation of petition for special permission to land
subfiles.from: Prospective guarantor
subfiles.about: Provides the guarantee form required for a passenger without a Japanese consular visa to land temporarily at Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: Translated form petitioning special landing permission for a passenger from San Francisco on the Chichibu Maru, with a guarantor's responsibilities.

subfiles.title: Maurine Carley inquiry about visas for an Asian voyage
subfiles.from: Maurine Carley, Cheyenne, Wyoming
subfiles.about: Asks whether visas and fees are required for brief stops in Japan, China, and Hong Kong during travel to the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: Maurine Carley asks whether visas are needed for a trip to the Philippines with one-day stops in Japan, China and Hong Kong (received May 1, 1935).

subfiles.title: Instruction transmitting Japanese Embassy note on the Marcus Show
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits a Japanese Embassy note acknowledging that the San Francisco consulate misunderstood the 1926 visa-waiver agreement in the Marcus Show case.
subfiles.summary: Instruction forwards the Japanese Embassy's December 24, 1934 note on the Marcus Show: the San Francisco consulate misunderstood the 1926 visa-waiver agreement.

subfiles.title: B. F. Keith Corporation letter thanking the Department for assistance
subfiles.from: Hardie Meakin, Resident Manager, B. F. Keith Corporation
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention R. B. Shipley
subfiles.about: Thanks the Department for its response concerning the Marcus Shows’ passport difficulties in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Meakin of the B. F. Keith Corporation thanks the Department for answering his Marcus Shows inquiry and forwards its letter to the show's management.

subfiles.title: Department letter to Sol Bloom on the Marcus Show visa dispute
subfiles.from: R. B. Shipley, Department of State
subfiles.about: Explains that the Marcus Show’s difficulties resulted from erroneous advice about the 1926 reciprocal visa-waiver agreement.
subfiles.summary: Department tells Sol Bloom the Marcus troupe took free thirty-day transit visas to avoid ten-dollar fees, was refused further extension, and Japan attributed it to the San Francisco consulate's misunderstanding.

subfiles.title: Department letter on the Marcus Show visa-waiver misunderstanding
subfiles.from: R. B. Shipley, Department of State
subfiles.about: Responds to earlier correspondence about the Marcus Show and the Japanese consulate’s misunderstanding of the reciprocal visa-waiver agreement.
subfiles.summary: Faint letter repeating that the Marcus Show's trouble arose from mistaken advice on visa fees; Japan's Embassy regretted it and told its San Francisco consul to take greater care.

subfiles.title: Department letter on the Marcus Show’s transit visas
subfiles.from: R. B. Shipley, Department of State
subfiles.about: Explains the Marcus Show’s use of transit visas and Japan’s acknowledgment of consular error.
subfiles.summary: Department says the Marcus Show's manager avoided about eight hundred dollars in visa fees using free transit visas, then had to leave when an extension was refused; Japan blamed a consulate misunderstanding.

subfiles.title: Department letter to Mr. Boehne on the Marcus Show
subfiles.from: R. B. Shipley, Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports the outcome of the Department’s inquiry into the Marcus Show’s visa and residence difficulties in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Department tells Mr. Boehne the Marcus show took free transit visas, left when an extension was denied, and Japan blamed its San Francisco consulate's misreading of the 1926 agreement.
